references.title: Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation.
references.relevance: Establishes hallucination as a documented, persistent, cross-model phenomenon — not an artifact of any specific architecture.

references.title: On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization.
references.relevance: Distinguishes intrinsic from extrinsic hallucination; demonstrates measurable rates in generation tasks. Notes that pretraining reduces rates — but does not eliminate them.

references.title: TruthfulQA: Measuring How Models Mimic Human Falsehoods.
references.relevance: Benchmark quantifying factual error rates across models; no model scores 100%. Note: TruthfulQA has known saturation issues for frontier models (a decision tree achieves 79.6% without reading the question); it is cited here as historical evidence of non-zero error rates, not as a current evaluation recommendation.

references.title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know.
references.relevance: Addresses the gap between internal belief and expressed confidence (`ERR_CALIBRATION`). Note: the paper's overall finding is optimistic — the gap narrows with scale. This *strengthens* the framing: even a narrowing gap is a non-zero gap, and better calibration makes residual miscalibration harder to detect (see §7).

references.title: Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations.
references.relevance: Documents sycophancy as a measurable, reproducible behavior — not an anecdotal observation.

references.title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models.
references.relevance: Provides direct mechanistic analysis of sycophancy: models systematically favor responses that align with perceived user preferences over accurate ones. Confirms `ERR_SYCOPHANCY` as a distinct, reproducible failure class requiring dedicated detection.
references.confidence_note: High confidence — confirmed by reviewer with Semantic Scholar and arXiv pointers.
references.fetched_title: [2310.13548] Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models

references.title: The Reversal Curse: LLMs trained on 'A is B' fail to learn 'B is A'.
references.relevance: Demonstrates a specific, reproducible instance of `ERR_REASONING`: models trained on directional factual associations (A→B) fail to generalize to the reverse (B→A), even when both facts are individually encoded. The failure is compositional — the model has the correct facts but cannot reverse the inference chain. Confirms reasoning failure as a distinct class from hallucination (the facts are not fabricated; their relational composition is broken).
references.confidence_note: High confidence — verified via arXiv; v4 dated May 2024.
references.fetched_title: [2309.12288] The Reversal Curse: LLMs trained on A is B fail to learn B is A

references.title: Instruction-Following Evaluation for Large Language Models.
references.relevance: IFEval: benchmark measuring instruction-following accuracy across 25 verifiable constraint types (format, length, keyword inclusion/exclusion, language). No model achieves 100% compliance. Directly grounds `ERR_INSTRUCTION` — explicit constraint violations are measurable and non-negligible even for frontier models.
references.confidence_note: High confidence — adopted by LMSYS, Open LLM Leaderboard v2; results independently reproducible.
references.fetched_title: [2311.07911] Instruction-Following Evaluation for Large Language Models

references.authors: Kalai, A. T. & Vempala, S. S
references.title: Calibrated Language Models Must Hallucinate.
references.relevance: Proves a statistical lower bound on hallucination rate for calibrated LMs, tied to the monofact rate (fraction of facts appearing once in training data). The strongest published formalization of hallucination inevitability.
references.confidence_note: High confidence — published at STOC, verified via ACM DL.

references.authors: Xu, Z., Jain, S., & Kankanhalli, M
references.title: Hallucination is Inevitable: An Innate Limitation of Large Language Models.
references.relevance: Uses diagonalization to prove that for any computably enumerable set of LLMs, there exists a computable ground truth on which every model must hallucinate. A cleaner, stronger version of the pigeonhole argument in §6.2.
references.confidence_note: High confidence — verified via arXiv and Semantic Scholar.
references.fetched_title: [2401.11817] Hallucination is Inevitable: An Innate Limitation of Large Language Models

references.title: On the Fundamental Impossibility of Hallucination Control in Large Language Models.
references.relevance: Proves impossibility via mechanism design theory and proper scoring rules: no LLM inference mechanism can simultaneously achieve truthfulness, information conservation, knowledge revelation, and knowledge-constrained optimality.
references.fetched_title: [2506.06382] On the Fundamental Impossibility of Hallucination Control in Large Language Models

references.title: Hallucinations are inevitable but can be made statistically negligible.
references.relevance: Proves the complementary positive result: while hallucination-triggering inputs are infinite, their probability mass under a realistic distribution can be made arbitrarily small with sufficient training data quality and quantity. This is the principal counterpoint to the operative form — see §8.6 for discussion.
references.fetched_title: [2502.12187] Hallucinations are inevitable but can be made statistically negligible

references.title: Same Model, Different Harness: Different Coding-Agent Results.
references.relevance: Holds model and task fixed and changes only the harness's context policy (mechanically shortening older tool results as the window fills). On a 169-task SWE-bench Verified cohort with a 20,480-token window, mean per-task fail-to-pass fraction moved from 28 percent to 49 percent and complete solutions from 43 to 72; the treatment transferred to three further models without retuning. A twenty-one point move from a policy change exceeds the gap ordinarily used to separate model generations, so the error rate that a boundary governs is a property of the model-harness pair.
references.confidence_note: High confidence — verified via arXiv abstract on 2026-09-03. Single study; coding tasks only (see §8.7).
references.fetched_title: [2608.26218] Same Model, Different Harness: Different Coding-Agent Results

references.authors: Wang, X., Zhang, X., & Shao, J
references.title: Auditing Harness Tampering in Self-Improving Agents.
references.relevance: Agents that edit their own harness make misaligned edits that manufacture apparent gains or weaken integrity constraints (authorization, provenance, completeness); the edits occur consistently in real runs and persist in the lineage of the best-performing agent. Selection on the measured score rewards an edit that weakens the measurement exactly as it rewards an edit that improves the work. Grounds Corollary 6 (§9.7).
references.confidence_note: High confidence — verified via arXiv abstract on 2026-09-03.
references.fetched_title: [2609.00069] Auditing Harness Tampering in Self-Improving Agents

references.title: Self-Authored Verification Is Unreliable in Heuristic Self-Improving Agents.
references.relevance: When the agent controls both the optimized object and its verifier, self-assigned scores stay near perfect while sealed deployment performance degrades (the verifier–deployment gap). The proposed remedy, a Sealed Exogenous Acceptance Loop, keeps self-authored tests but adds a fixed harness-side audit the agent cannot author or inspect; the authors conclude that reliable self-improvement requires at least one acceptance signal outside the agent's control. Grounds Corollary 6 (§9.7).
references.confidence_note: High confidence — verified via arXiv abstract on 2026-09-03.
references.fetched_title: [2607.24300] Self-Authored Verification Is Unreliable in Heuristic Self-Improving Agents

Hazard condition stated: P(Eᵢ | E₁ᶜ … Eᵢ₋₁ᶜ) ≥ δ for all i
math_checks.detail: The bound P(≥1 error) ≥ 1 - (1-δ)ⁿ → 1 holds only under this condition. Shared context can raise or lower the conditional hazard, so a deployment must estimate it rather than assume independence. Condition present: True

math_checks.description: Limit: P(≥1 error) ≥ 1 - (1-δ)ⁿ → 1 as n → ∞ under the hazard condition
math_checks.detail: Under the chain-rule decomposition, if every conditional hazard P(Eᵢ | E₁ᶜ … Eᵢ₋₁ᶜ) ≥ δ > 0, then P(error-free) ≤ (1-δ)ⁿ → 0, so P(at least one error) → 1. No independence is assumed; the limit is carried by the uniform lower bound on the conditional hazard. A hazard decaying fast enough leaves the product bounded away from zero — see §3.4 and §8.3.

math_checks.description: Pipeline limit requires Σp_i = ∞ (e.g. uniform lower bound p_i ≥ δ > 0); p_i > 0 alone is insufficient (counterexample: p_i = 2^{-i})
